text: A 12-year-old touches the wall. The scoreboard flashes a new national age group record. It is not his first this season. It is not even his fifth. This is the story of Aiden Tan, a swimmer from San Ramón Valley Aquatics in California, who spent the summer of 2025 doing something almost no swimmer his age has ever done. Breaking national records again and again in different strokes at different distances that small local meets most people never heard of. By the time his 11-12 age group ended, Tan had broken seven national age group records in a single summer. That number alone should stop you. Most elite age group swimmers are thrilled to break one national record in their entire time in that bracket. Tan broke seven before he even turned 13. It started well before that summer. Tan already held five national age group records in the 10 and under category, meaning this was not a sudden breakthrough. It was a continuation of a pattern that had been building for years. The 2025 record run began in the 200-meter individual medley. At the T.Y. or GO International Challenge in Fresno, California, Tan swam two minutes 12.80 seconds, breaking the previous record of two 13.59 set by Richard Papploski back in 2019. Papploski's record had stood for six years. Tan lowered it by nearly eight tenths of a second, a significant margin in a four-stroke event that punishes any weakness. That swim alone would have made for a strong season. Tan kept going. At a small local meet in Saratoga, California, he broke two more national records on the same day. The 50-yard fly and the 200-yard I.M. in the 50 fly, he swam 22.85 seconds, breaking a record of 22.87 that had been set by Thomas Hylman in 2019. Hylman's own record had been a massive half-second jump over the previous mark when he set it. Hylman went on to qualify for the 2024 Paris Olympic team at age 17. Tan broke his record at age 12. The pattern continued into the summer's biggest meets. At the far Western championships, in what his father said would likely be his final national age group record before aging up. Tan swam 24.95 seconds in the 50-meter freestyle. That broke a record of 24.98 that had stood since 2017, set by Ronald Del Masio. Tan's own best time in the event just weeks earlier had been 25.12, which had only ranked him fourth in the country for his age group. He dropped nearly two tenths and became the new national standard in less than a month. He also broke records in the 100-yard back in the 100-yard I.M. before aging out of the 11-12 bracket, bringing his total for the age group to 7. Combined with his five records from the 10 and under category, Tan has now set 12 national age group records across two separate age brackets, even at meets where he did not break a national record, Tan kept posting best times. At sectionals in Novato, he did not add to his record total, but he still swam a lifetime best of two, 1239 in the 200-meter backstroke. That is the part of his season that gets less attention than the record-breaking swims, but it matters just as much. It shows a swimmer who was racing nearly every weekend and still finding improvement even in the meets without headlines. Over one stretch, Tan competed in six of seven consecutive weekends, a demanding schedule for any age group athlete. What makes this run stand out is not just the number of records, it is the range of events. Tan did not specialize in one stroke or one distance. He broke records in freestyle, butterfly, backstroke, and the individual medley across both short course yards and long course meters. Most swimmers, even elite ones, find one or two strokes where they excel. Tan has shown elite level speed across nearly the entire event lineup. This range matters more than it might first appear. The four competitive strokes, freestyle, butterfly, backstroke, and breaststroke, each demand different muscle patterns, different breathing rhythms, and different technical skills. The individual medley combines all four in a single race, which means a swimmer has to be technically sound in every stroke, not just strong in one. Coach is often view I am success as one of the clearest signs of an all-around, technically complete swimmer, rather than a one-event specialist who got lucky with body type. His progress within events tells the same story. At a memorial day, meat hosted by Tiger Aquatics, Tan swam the 200 IM in two, 13.89, moving him to second on the all-time list for his age group, just three tenths behind Papploski's previous record. At that point, he had already dropped more than three seconds from a 217.37, he had swam only weeks earlier in April. He also moved into the top ten all-time in the 50 fly with a time of 27th more than a second faster than the 28-pointer he had swam the year before. Swimming coaches and analysts who track age group progression have pointed to a pattern in swimmers who dominate the 1112 bracket this deeply. According to reporting from swim swam before Tan, roughly a dozen boys had produced five or more top 20 all-time swims in long course meters at this age. More than half of those who were old enough to qualify went on to make a senior national team. That does not guarantee anything about Tan's future, but it places him in a small group of swimmers whose age group dominance has historically translated into senior level success. None of this happened without setbacks along the way. Tan has swam for multiple clubs during his development, moving between Dart, A now disbanded club called Crow, and his current team, San Ramon Valley Aquatics, along with a brief stint with Phoenix Swim team. Club changes are common in competitive youth swimming, as families look for the right coaching fit and training environment as a swimmer grows. The obvious question surrounding any swimmer this fast this young is what comes next. Age group swimming and elite senior swimming are different sports in many ways. Puberty changes bodies unpredictably. Growth spurts can help or disrupt technique. Training loads have to increase carefully to avoid injury and burnout. Many age group record holders never make a senior national team, some flame out from overtraining. Others simply get passed by later developing swimmers with different genetics, but the swimmers who do make that jump often share one trait Tan has already shown. Range. A swimmer who is fast in only one stroke can be caught by specialists who focus entirely on that event. A swimmer who is fast across freestyle, butterfly, backstroke, and the IAM has more paths forward and more room to specialize later once his body settles into its adult shape. Tan's own results this season point to steady, structured improvement rather than one lucky swim. His times dropped gradually across the year, month after month rather than arriving in one unexplainable jump. That kind of pattern is usually the sign of solid training rather than a flute performance. For now, Tan moves into the 1314 age group, a new bracket with a new set of records to chase and a new group of competitors closer to his own developing size and strength. The national age group record book will no longer measure him against 11 and 12-year-old. It will measure him against some of the best 13 and 14-year-old swimmers in the country, many of whom are already committing to top college programs. Whether I, Tan, becomes a senior national team swimmer is a question that will take years to answer. What is already true right now? Is that a 12-year-old from California spent one summer setting seven national records across four different strokes? Something almost no swimmer his age has ever accomplished. Age group swimming history offers a useful reminder here too. Not every prodigy follows a straight line to the top. Some age group record holders plateau in their teenage years, while others who were far less dominant at 12 end up making Olympic teams a decade later. Records at this age are a strong signal of talent and training quality, not a guarantee of what comes next. That uncertainty is part of what makes following a swimmer like Tan interesting. No one, including Tan himself, knows exactly how this story ends. Do you think Aidan Tan keeps up this record breaking pace into his teenage years? Could he be swimming for a spot on a senior national team within the next few years? Drop your prediction in the comments below. I read every single one. If you want to follow Aidan Tan's next chapter as he takes on the 13-14 age group, subscribe now. The fastest 12-year-old in the country just aged up, and the record book is about to get another new name.
